sentences.text: Odval was quiet for a moment, thinking.
Bata sat very still on Chuluun and did not interrupt.
He had never seen his grandmother worried before.
Then she said, "The ovoo on Bogd Hill.
It is forty minutes northeast.
There is a shepherd's shelter behind it — a small stone hut for storms.
Your father and I used it two years ago.
We will drive the horses that way.
If we go now, we may make it before the rain."
She turned Chuluun's head with the flat of her hand and started him moving.
Bata followed.
The horses, sensing the change of wind, moved more quickly on their own — they knew a storm was coming, better than any human.
The wind began to rise.
Bata could smell the rain now — the cold clean smell of the storm coming across empty land.
They made it.
Just.

The first heavy drops began to fall as they crested Bogd Hill and Bata saw the ovoo for the first time — the great pile of grey stones his grandmother had spoken of, with tall wooden poles rising from the middle, and the long blue prayer scarves — khadag — snapping horizontally in the wind.
Behind it, dug into the hillside, was the shelter she had promised — a small low hut of piled stone with a wooden door and a shallow overhang for the horses.
Odval showed him how to tie the horses to the long rope that ran between two posts under the overhang, so the wind would not spook them off.
Then she opened the wooden door of the hut, and they went inside just as the sky broke.
Inside the hut it was dry and dim and smelled of old smoke.
It was very small — just a stone floor, a low stone hearth, a rough bench, two shuttered windows.
Whoever had left it last had left dry argal — dried yak dung fuel — stacked neatly by the hearth, and a small bundle of tinder.
Odval started a small fire while Bata unpacked the tea and the dried meat and the flat bread they had brought in their saddlebags.
Outside, the rain became a proper storm — heavy, sideways, loud on the stone roof.
"How long will it last?" Bata asked.
Odval looked out through a crack in the shutter.
She said, "Maybe two hours.
Maybe till morning.
We will not know until it stops.
We are safe here.
The horses are under cover.
We have tea.
This is fine."
They ate.
Odval boiled water for tea, and made it the way she always made it — with milk and a pinch of salt.
They drank it slowly.
Bata's small saddle sat on the earth floor beside him.
In the firelight, the old leather looked almost red.
The small triangle brand on the underside caught the light.
He touched it with his fingertip.
Odval saw him do it.
She said, "You should know what happened to him.
Your great-great-grandfather.
Since you are riding his saddle." She sat back against the stone wall and pulled her del closer around her.
"He died in a storm.
A winter storm — a zud — when he was fifty-eight.
He rode out to bring in a young horse that had wandered.
He found the horse.
He was bringing it back.
But the storm came in faster than he had planned.
He was two hours from home when it hit.
He did not make it back."
Bata was quiet.
He looked at the saddle.
Odval said, "I tell you this because you should know.
Storms are not always survived.
He knew this.
He rode anyway, because the horse would have died alone.
That is the choice a herder sometimes has to make.
You will have to make it too, someday.
I am not telling you the story to frighten you.
I am telling you because this saddle came home without him.
His son — my grandfather — rode back out three days later, when the storm passed, and found him and the young horse.
The horse was alive.
My great-grandfather had wrapped his own del around it before he died.
The saddle came home tied to that horse."
She looked at Bata.
"Every rider in this family since then has ridden this saddle at least once.
It is our way of remembering that he did not come back alone.
He came back with the horse he went to save.
This is what the saddle is for."
Bata did not know what to say.
Outside the hut, the storm cracked.
The horses under the overhang whinnied once, close and afraid.
Odval put out her hand and rested it on Bata's shoulder.
She said, "Do not be afraid tonight.
He rode out into a much worse storm than this.
You are riding out into a summer rain.
We will wait.
It will pass." And in the small warm hut, they waited.
